shared_context.topic: hepatitis A IgM test result interpretation

atoms.1: A non-reactive result for the hepatitis A IgM (anti-HAV IgM) test means that the test did not detect any antibodies to the hepatitis A virus in the patient's blood.
atoms.2: This can be interpreted in several ways depending on the clinical context.
atoms.3: In the context of acute viral hepatitis, a non-reactive anti-HAV IgM result can be seen in patients who have recently contracted hepatitis A, but the immune response has not yet been triggered, usually in the very early phase of the infection.
atoms.4: A non-reactive anti-HAV IgM result can be seen in patients with non-A, non-B hepatitis or other forms of viral hepatitis where the immune response is directed against a different viral antigen.
atoms.5: A positive result for anti-HAV IgM retesting was associated with high initial cutoff index (COI) for anti-HAV IgM (≥0.5) in a study conducted among initially seronegative patients.
atoms.6: A positive result for anti-HAV IgM retesting was associated with low serum total bilirubin (<1.4 mg/dl) in a study conducted among initially seronegative patients.
atoms.7: A positive result for anti-HAV IgM retesting was associated with low platelet count (<165 × 10^3/μl) in a study conducted among initially seronegative patients.
atoms.8: The association of a positive result for anti-HAV IgM retesting with the mentioned factors was not statistically significant on multivariate analysis.
atoms.9: Only 0.3% of patients tested positive for anti-HEV IgM in a study examining the prevalence of hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection among patients with acute non-A, non-B hepatitis in Central Brazil.
atoms.10: HEV may be responsible for a small percentage of acute hepatitis cases.
atoms.11: A non-reactive result for hepatitis A IgM does not necessarily rule out the possibility of viral hepatitis.
atoms.12: Further testing, including evaluating other serological markers, should be considered to determine the cause of the patient's symptoms.
atoms.13: Norkrans G, Nilsson LA, Frösner G, Wahl M, Iwarson S. conducted a study on serum immunoglobulin levels in hepatitis non-A, non-B: a comparison with hepatitis A and B.
atoms.14: Findor JA, Lafage M, Bruch Igartua EM, Domecq P, Firpo AM, Domecq RB. published an article on acute non-A, non-B viral hepatitis.
atoms.15: Psichogiou M, Tzala E, Boletis J, Zakopoulou N, Loutradi A, Maliori M, et al. conducted a study on hepatitis E virus infection in individuals at high risk of transmission of non-A, non-B hepatitis and sexually transmitted diseases.
atoms.16: Shin HP, Lee JI, Jung SW, Cha JM, Joo KR, Kang SY. published a study on factors for predicting positive results for anti-HAV IgM retesting among initially seronegative patients.
atoms.17: Freitas NR, Santana EB, Silva AM, Silva SM, Teles SA, Gardinali NR, et al. conducted a study on hepatitis E virus infection in patients with acute non-A, non-B, non-C hepatitis in Central Brazil.
atoms.18: Darwish MA, Shaker M, al-Kady AM. published a study on non-A, non-B viral hepatitis in Egypt.

snippets.output: A non-reactive result for the hepatitis A IgM (anti-HAV IgM) test means that the test did not detect any antibodies to the hepatitis A virus in the blood.

In the context of acute viral hepatitis, a non-reactive hepatitis A IgM result can occur if hepatitis A was contracted very recently but the immune response has not yet been triggered, usually in the very early phase of infection.
A non-reactive anti-HAV IgM result can be seen in patients with non-A, non-B hepatitis or other forms of viral hepatitis where the immune response is directed against a different viral antigen.

A non-reactive hepatitis A IgM (anti-HAV IgM) result means the test did not detect antibodies to the hepatitis A virus in the blood, and its interpretation depends on the clinical context. In the context of acute viral hepatitis, a non-reactive anti-HAV IgM result can occur very early after hepatitis A infection before the immune response has been triggered, or in non-A, non-B hepatitis or other forms of viral hepatitis where the immune response is directed against a different viral antigen.
A positive anti-HAV IgM retest result was associated with a high initial anti-HAV IgM cutoff index (COI ≥0.5) in a study of initially seronegative patients.
A positive result for anti-HAV IgM retesting was associated with low serum total bilirubin (<1.4 mg/dl) in a study conducted among initially seronegative patients.
A positive anti-HAV IgM retest result was associated with a low platelet count of less than 165 × 10^3/μl in a study of initially seronegative patients.

In a study of initially seronegative patients, a positive anti-HAV IgM retest was associated with a high initial anti-HAV IgM cutoff index (COI ≥0.5), low serum total bilirubin (<1.4 mg/dl), and low platelet count (<165 × 10^3/μl), but these associations were not statistically significant on multivariate analysis.
Only 0.3% of patients tested positive for anti-HEV IgM in a study examining the prevalence of hepatitis E virus infection among patients with acute non-A, non-B hepatitis in Central Brazil.

Only 0.3% of patients tested positive for anti-HEV IgM in a study examining the prevalence of hepatitis E virus infection among patients with acute non-A, non-B hepatitis in Central Brazil, suggesting that hepatitis E virus may be responsible for a small percentage of acute hepatitis cases.

A non-reactive hepatitis A IgM result does not necessarily rule out the possibility of viral hepatitis. Further testing, including evaluation of other serological markers, should be considered to determine the cause of the symptoms.
